title: memcpy-contention-microburst-postmortem-and-hotfix-validation
summary: On 2025-06-11 we observed repeated sub-second microburst tail-latency spikes (95th->99.9th) on a subset of Dedicated clusters serving medium-context chat workloads. After investigation, the immediate root cause was high memcpy contention on the host NIC RX/TX path induced by a new multi-tenant KV cache replication path that used synchronous memcpy in the hotpath during model variant switches. A hotfix that changed the replication to async off-thread memcpy + backpressure reduced 99.9th latency by ~65% for affected routes. This doc summarizes findings, profiling artifacts, hotfix validation, customer impact and follow-ups.
impact: Incidents: 3 customer escalations over 24h, SLO misses (95th latency SLO violated intermittently for 2 customers). Affected: ~12 Dedicated pods across two regions. Observable metrics: 95th latency increased from 120ms to 400–550ms during bursts; 99.9th reached 1.2–1.6s. CPU steal and softirq counters spiked on hosts where NIC memcpy dominated. No data loss; model outputs remained correct. Financial/contract: potential SLA credits for two Dedicated accounts if repeated; customer experience degraded for low-latency products.

investigation:
Initial clues: spikes aligned with model-switch events (pin->variant fallback) and with higher-than-usual cache replication rate (new cheap-write replication introduced in May). Engineer notes from observability: high softirq, elevated netdev_stats.tx_dropped on some NICs and CPU runqueue length spikes concurrent with tail-latency bursts.
Steps taken:
- Captured perf samples and flamegraphs (user+kernel) for request-handling threads during a burst window.
- Deployed eBPF scripts to measure memcpy syscall counts and durations per thread.
- Correlated application traces (trace IDs) with kernel-level samples to ensure hotpath alignment.
Findings: a tight loop in replication code path executed synchronous memcpy large-block copies (8–64 KB) while holding a replication mutex. When model variant switch triggered multiple replicas to update (N=3), the combined memcpy load saturated NIC CPU offload path and consumed host CPU cycles via softirqs, blocking request polling threads. The synchronous nature meant request-handling threads frequently waited on the replication mutex or queued behind softirq processing, amplifying tail-latency.
profiling_artifacts:
Key artifacts saved to: confluence perf folder (link above) and GH gist references in PR. Short summary of profiles:
- Flamegraph (user+kernel): top kernel symbols: memcpy, net_rx_action, napi_poll, softirq_raise.
- eBPF counters: memcpy_count per-second went from baseline ~120/s to 520/s during bursts on affected hosts.
- Stack traces: replication_worker -> memcpy -> kernel memory ops -> napi_poll.
- Heatmap: bursts aligned tightly with model switch trigger times (0–300ms after switch event).
Attached raw artifacts: perf.data.gz (saved), ebpf-memcpy-counts.csv, flamegraph.svg (all in linked_artifacts).
root_cause: Design regression in multi-tenant KV cache replication introduced synchronous large-block memcpy in the model-variant switch code path. This synchronous copy was executed on threads that could be scheduled on the same CPUs handling NIC softirq processing, causing host-level contention and amplified tail-latency. Secondary contributors: lack of replication-rate backpressure and no per-pod memcpy offload threshold. New replication path was rolled out to Dedicated pools in May without microbenchmarking under realistic multi-variant churn.
reproducer:
Local reproducer steps (recommended to replicate in a perf lab, not prod):
1) Start cluster with 3 replica workers and enable new replication path (env REPL_V2=on).
2) Preload KV cache with 200k keys (use provided loader script).
3) Create synthetic model-switch workload: send 50 concurrent model-switch requests across 3 pods at t=0, repeated every 30s for 10 rounds.
4) Observe host-level metrics: softirq, runqueue length, memcpy_count with eBPF. Use scripts/bench/memcopy_burst.sh.
Notes: a lightweight reproducer included in GH under scripts/bench; it uses iperf-like burster to mimic NIC pressure and triggers variant-switch flows.
hotfix_and_rollback:
Hotfix (PR #1487) summary:
- Change replication copies from synchronous memcpy in request thread to async off-thread memcpy performed by dedicated replication worker pool.
- Add a bounded output queue and adaptive backpressure: when queue depth > 16, replication requests are rate-limited and requests can take cached-stale path for up to 500ms.
- Add per-pod memcpy-size histogram logging and a circuit-breaker that falls back to compact-delta replication if memcpy cost exceeds threshold.
Validation performed on canary: enabled for 6 canary pods for 12 hours with synthetic churn; measured latency percentiles and host softirq/cpu.
Rollback plan: standard deploy rollback via orchestration if 5xx increase or 95th latency regresses beyond baseline +20% within 30m of rollout. No rollback needed; hotfix promoted after canary metrics passed.
validation:
Quantitative results after hotfix rollout:
- 95th latency: baseline 120ms -> pre-hotfix bursts 400–550ms -> post-hotfix 140–160ms on affected routes.
- 99.9th latency: pre-hotfix 1.2–1.6s -> post-hotfix 380–520ms.
- memcpy_count peak reduced by ~72% on affected hosts; softirq CPU usage dropped 60%.
- No regression in throughput for normal traffic; slight increase in average replication lag (0ms -> 60ms median) during very high churn, within acceptable SLAs.
Validation methods: A/B with stable and canary pools, synthetic churn tester, end-to-end traces to ensure no functional regression, load testing up to 1.25x expected peak.
customer_communication: On 2025-06-13 we sent a targeted incident notification to the two impacted Dedicated customers with: incident timeline, root cause summary, mitigation steps, and planned follow-ups. Customers were offered 1:1 technical calls; two accepted and we reviewed the fix and test evidence. We proactively flagged potential future risks and offered configuration toggles (disable REPL_V2 or set replication_rate cap). No immediate SLA credits requested as the hotfix resolved repeatable regressions; Customer Success will follow up to confirm satisfaction.

Short-term (next 2 weeks):
- Add unit/microbench suite for replication path including large memcpy scenarios (owner: Marc).
- Ship telemetry: memcpy histograms and replication-queue depth per pod (owner: Zoe).
- Add canary gating: require replication microbench before Dedicated rollout (owner: Priya).
Medium-term (quarter):
- Reimplement replication to use zero-copy page remap where possible and evaluate io_uring for offloaded copies.
- Design per-tenant replication rate controls in control plane.
- Add automated chaos tests simulating multi-variant churn.
Long-term:
- Re-evaluate hotpath threading model; reduce host softirq coupling by pinning replication workers to non-NIC CPUs.
Owners and deadlines listed in the separate follow-up ticket JIRA-RT-6789.
notes_and_lessons:
- Hotpath changes with host-level side effects must include kernel-level microbenching (softirq, memcpy cost).
- Perf+eBPF remains the fastest way to map application-level events to kernel-level contention; keep that tooling in the standard SRE runbook.
- Canary rollouts should include high-churn synthetic workloads that mimic model variant switching, not only steady-state throughput.
- Consider explicit 'expensive-copy' annotation on code paths so runtime can prefer incremental/compact encodings.
- Cross-team review (platform + infra + sRE) required for changes touching replication, NIC handling, and threading.
conclusion: Root cause: synchronous large-block memcpy in new replication code path causing host-level softirq and memcpy contention, producing microburst tail-latency spikes. Hotfix (async off-thread memcpy + backpressure) mitigated the immediate issue and restored SLOs. Action items assigned to harden replication path and improve pre-rollout perf tests. Postmortem accepted by oncall lead and eng leadership.
